title: The Orbit of the Single Outer Napoleon Construction
content: The parent entry napoleons-theorem-oq-03 composes the outer and inner Napoleon constructions and shows the composite annihilates a triangle's shape, collapsing it to the centroid. Its first open question asks the opposite: what happens when you iterate the single outer construction T_out? This file answers it. The doubled outer triangle T_out²(z) turns out to be the half-turn (180° rotation) of the single outer triangle T_out(z) about their common centroid g. A third application undoes that rotation, so T_out³ = T_out and T_out⁴ = T_out²: the orbit is periodic with period (dividing) two. On a nondegenerate triangle the period is exactly two.
mathContext: $T_{out}^2(z)_k = 2g - T_{out}(z)_k$ with $g=(z_0+z_1+z_2)/3$; hence $T_{out}^3=T_{out}$ and the orbit $\{T_{out}^n(z): n\ge 1\}$ is a two-cycle pivoting about the fixed centroid.

title: One Non-Ring Fact: a² = -1/12
content: Because every Napoleon vertex map is ℂ-affine, the iterated maps are ℂ-polynomials and every identity in the file is a polynomial statement. The only fact that is not pure ring arithmetic is that the displacement coefficient a = i√3/6 squares to -1/12. This follows from i² = -1 (Complex.I_sq) and √3² = 3 (Real.sq_sqrt, lifted to ℂ). It is used in exactly one place — the per-vertex reflection law — through a single deterministic linear_combination.

title: Half-Turn Equivariance Is the Engine
content: The key structural lemma napCenter_halfTurn says that reflecting both endpoints of a side through a center g reflects the resulting Napoleon center through g: napCenter(2g−b, 2g−c) = 2g − napCenter(b,c). Crucially this is a pure ring identity — the displacement coefficient a cancels symbolically, so the equivariance holds regardless of the value of a. The period-two phenomenon rides entirely on this symmetry together with centroid preservation; the specific value a² = -1/12 is only needed to identify T_out²(z) as the half-turn in the first place.
mathContext: $\mathrm{napCenter}(2g-b,2g-c)=2g-\mathrm{napCenter}(b,c)$ for every center $g$ — a constant-free reflection symmetry.

title: The Point-Reflection Law Hₖ = 2g − Gₖ
content: Unfolding the doubled construction one vertex at a time, the difference between Hₖ = T_out²(z)ₖ and the half-turn 2g − Gₖ factors as a linear expression in z times (a² + 1/12), which vanishes by disp_sq. Each of the three vertices closes with a single linear_combination (linear coefficient) * disp_sq, with the coefficients cyclically permuted. This is the one place the arithmetic fact a² = -1/12 enters; everything afterward is ring rewriting.

title: Period Two Without Brute Force
content: Rather than expanding the triple composition T_out³ (a degree-4 polynomial identity in the displacement coefficient), the proof composes two clean facts. Writing G = T_out(z) and H = T_out²(z) = half-turn of G, a further application of T_out and the half-turn equivariance give T_out(H)ₖ = 2g − napCenter(Gᵢ,Gⱼ) = 2g − Hₖ = Gₖ. Hence T_out³ = T_out, and applying T_out once more yields T_out⁴ = T_out² — the orbit stabilises into a two-cycle. The iterate form T_out^[4] = T_out^[2] is recorded as well.
mathContext: $T_{out}^3 = T_{out}$, so $T_{out}^4 = T_{out}^2$ and $T_{out}^{n}(z)$ for $n\ge 1$ has period dividing two.

title: Exactly Two, and Why the Hypothesis Is Needed
content: Doubling is not idempotent: T_out²(z) = T_out(z) would force every outer vertex Gₖ onto the centroid g, i.e. the outer Napoleon triangle collapsing to a point. So on any nondegenerate triangle the period is exactly two — contrasting sharply with the parent's outer∘inner composition, which always collapses. The fixed-point sanity check T_out(0,0,0) = (0,0,0) shows the degenerate locus is genuinely there and the nondegeneracy hypothesis cannot be dropped.
mathContext: $T_{out}^2(z)=T_{out}(z) \iff G_k = g$ for all $k$ (collapse). Nondegenerate $\Rightarrow$ exact period two.
